newsitem.title: USA: Amgen falls sharply as company warns of slower growth.
newsitem.headline: Amgen falls sharply as company warns of slower growth.

text.p: Amgen Inc. stock fell sharply Tuesday after the company said sales would slow for the rest of the year and analysts warned its days as a high-growth investment could be over.

In a Securities Exchange Commission filing, the world's biggest biotechnology company said sales of its No. 1 drug, the red blood cell-boosting agent Epogen, would grow at a rate slower than previously forecast due to changes in government reimbursement policies.

Amgen further warned that sales growth of its only other drug, Neupogen -- which boosts white blood cell count in chemotherapy patients and others with compromised immune systems -- would also slow from 1996 levels because of reduced demand from AIDS patients.
Amgen stock tumbled $6.9375 to a new year low of $50.1875, and was the most actively traded issue on Nasdaq with volume of over 22.8 million shares.

Amgen Chairman Gordon Binder said in an interview the reduced sales expectations would have only a modest impact on earnings in 1997. But several analysts said it could be the start of a prolonged slowdown for the company.
Amgen's two drugs generate more than $2 billion in annual revenues. They have made Amgen a rare success story in the biotechnology industry.

Amgen is expected next year to introduce a new drug for hepatitis and another advanced drug for chemotherapy patients. But the market for each is limited, and hopes are dimming for a weight-loss drug it has in development, analysts said.

"The company has two great drugs, but they don't have a lot behind them," said Robert LeBoyer, analyst with investment bank Brown Brothers Harriman. "They need to have another blockbuster, or a string of base hits, but there's nothing in sight that fits that bill. It's hard to see where future sales growth will come from."

While Epogen has been the biggest source of earnings for Amgen -- its sales last year grew 21 percent -- the company has been forecasting an eventual sales slowdown. But Amgen said Tuesday that would happen sooner than expected because of stricter Medicare policies.
Under the new policies that take effect Sept. 1, fewer patients will qualify for reimbursement for Epogen. Doctors have started taking marginal patients off the drug or reducing their doses.
Last month, Amgen said it believed it could offset that decline by encouraging increased doses in other patients who fall well within the range allowed for reimbursement.

However, Mongtomery Securities analyst David Crosson said Amgen will have trouble continuing that practice as concern over health care costs mount and more studies come out showing limited benefits of both Epogen and Neupogen at high dosages.

Neupogen sales have started to suffer as AIDS patients find other drugs to keep them healthy, and Crosson said some cancer patients may also start to see that drug has limited benefits. He cited some studies that suggest Neupogen can be just as effective at a dosing level half of what is typically prescribed.
"Amgen is a value stock at the moment. It's not a growth stock anymore," said Alex To of investment bank Donaldson Lufkin and Jenrette.
